questions.q: This program should display a rectangle of * characters. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and type 3, then 4.
Every row holds the same number of * characters.
Move one line; do not delete it.

hint.think: Look at where row is emptied, and how many times that happens.
walk: The rows are getting longer, so something is being kept from the row before.
Work out what row holds at the start of each outer turn.
Decide which loop the emptying line belongs inside.

questions.starter:
rows = int(input())
width = int(input())
row = ""
for r in range(rows):
    for c in range(width):
        row = row + "*"
    print(row)

tests.why: The rows grew longer and longer, because row was only emptied once, before the first row was built.
With one row the mistake is hidden, which is why one test is never enough.
Both rows have to be the same length, so row starts empty again on every outer turn.

questions.fb: A variable rebuilt on every outer turn has to be emptied on every outer turn, inside the outer loop.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every row from 1 up to and including that number, work out the row number multiplied by 1, then by 2, and so on up to the number. Display each row's answers on one line.

teach.say: Numbers have to be turned into text with str() before + can join them onto a line being built up.

lines: Create line and set it to no characters at all.
Count 1, 2, 3 in turn.
Join the counter multiplied by 5, and then a space, onto line.
Display the finished line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, never less than 1.
One space between the numbers on a line.
The number typed in says how many lines there are and how many numbers are on each line.

hint.think: Each number on a line is the outer counter multiplied by the inner counter.

questions.starter: # Read a number, then display the multiplication square

tests.why: Both loops run from 1, not 0. A row of zeros means one of them started at 0.
A number of 1 gives one line holding 1 multiplied by 1.
Four lines of four numbers. Three lines means both ranges stopped one turn too early.
The row number stays still while the inner loop runs, so the outer counter belongs in the multiplication too.

questions.fb: Two counters multiplied together, built into a line of text. This is how a grid of values is displayed.

questions.q: Press Run. Type 4, then 5, then 9, pressing Enter after each one.

teach.say: A whole program reads its values, collects them up, and works the answer out at the end. Anything that needs the finished total belongs after the loop, where it runs once.

brief: Nothing is marked on this one.
Three numbers go in and two lines come out.
questions.starter:
total = 0
for i in range(3):
    n = int(input())
    total = total + n
print(total)
print(round(total / 3, 1))
lines: Create total and set it to 0.
Take three turns, one for each number.
Read a number and turn it into a whole number.
Add it to total.
Display the finished total.
Display the average, rounded to one decimal place.
questions.fb: Read, collect, then work it out. The average could not be worked out inside the loop, because the total was not finished yet.

questions.q: What will this program display?
brief: Read every line before you choose.

teach.say: Lines inside the loop run on every turn. The line after the loop runs once, when the total is finished.

questions.fb: Three indented lines give three lines of output, and the last line of the program adds the fourth.

questions.q: Change the program so the average is rounded to 1 decimal place.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
One line of output, which is the rounded average.

hint.think: round() is given the number and how many decimal places to keep.

questions.starter:
how_many = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(how_many):
    total = total + int(input())
print(total / how_many)

tests.why: A long row of decimals means the division is being displayed without round().
One number is its own average, and / always gives a decimal, so 7.0 and not 7.
Rounding to 1 decimal place keeps one digit after the point.

questions.fb: round() takes two things: the value and how many decimal places to keep.

questions.q: Finish the program so it adds up only the numbers above 0.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Exactly 0 is not above 0.
One line of output, which is the total.

hint.think: The gap is the question the if asks about the number just read.

questions.starter:
how_many = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(how_many):
    n = int(input())
    if ____:
        total = total + n
print(total)

tests.why: The -20 is left out while the three numbers above 0 are added.
Exactly 0 is not above 0, so it is skipped along with the -20.
None of them is above 0, so the total stays at 0 and that 0 still has to be displayed.
Every number above 0 is added, repeats included.

questions.fb: An if inside the loop is what makes a total add up some of the numbers and ignore the rest.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Add them up. Work out their average. Display the total. Then display the average on the next line.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Round the average to 1 decimal place.
Two lines of output: the total, then the average.

hint.think: The average needs the finished total, so it is worked out after the loop.
walk: Read how many numbers there are.
Add each number to the total inside the loop.
Display the total after the loop.
Divide the total by how many there were, round it, and display it.

questions.starter: # Read the numbers, then display the total and the average

tests.why: The total is a whole number and the average is rounded to one decimal place.
One number is its own average, and / gives a decimal, so 7.0 and not 7.
A long row of decimals on the second line means the round() is missing.
Divide by how many there were, not by a number written into the program.

questions.fb: The total grows inside the loop and the average is worked out after it, from the finished total.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. Work out which numbers from 1 up to and including it divide into it exactly. Display those numbers, one on each line.
brief: The user types in one whole number, never less than 1.
A number divides exactly when the remainder is 0.
The number typed in is always displayed, because it divides into itself.
1 is always displayed too.

hint.think: Try every number from 1 upwards in turn, and ask what the remainder is each time.

questions.starter: # Read a number, then display every number that divides into it exactly

tests.why: 4 and 5 leave a remainder, so they are left out.
Only 1 and the number itself divide into 7, so two lines come out.
One line only, because 1 divides into itself and there is nothing else to try.
A missing 12 means the loop stopped one turn too early.

questions.fb: % gives the remainder, and a remainder of 0 is how a program asks whether one number goes into another exactly.

questions.q: Ask the user for a whole number. For every counter from 1 to 10, work out the number multiplied by the counter. Display a line in the form [number] times [counter] is [answer].
brief: The user types in one whole number.
Ten lines of output, one for each counter from 1 to 10.
One space either side of times and either side of is.

hint.think: Every number in the message has to become text before + can join it on.

questions.starter: # Read a number, then display its times table up to 10

tests.why: Ten lines, and the counter has to reach 10, so the range stops past it.
The number typed in stays the same on every line while the counter changes.
A 0 gives ten lines of 0, and the counter still has to count up through them.

questions.fb: A loop that builds one sentence per turn is how most lists of results are displayed.

questions.q: This program should display the total of all the numbers typed in. Find the mistake and put it right.
brief: Press Run first and read the error message.
The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
One line of output, which is the total.

hint.think: Read the error. input() hands back text, whatever the user typed.

questions.starter:
how_many = int(input())
total = 0
for i in range(how_many):
    n = input()
    total = total + n
print(total)

tests.why: A TypeError here means a number was added to text. The line read inside the loop needs int() round it.
Casting has to happen as the value comes in, before the adding.
Once every number is cast, the negative one lowers the total as it should.
Zeros work the same as any other number once they are whole numbers.

questions.fb: The first line was cast and the one inside the loop was not. Every input() that feeds a sum needs its own int().

questions.q: Ask the user for how many numbers there are. Then ask for that many whole numbers. Display the total of the ones above 0. Then display how many are below 0 on the next line. Then display the average of all of them on the next line.
brief: The user types in a whole number saying how many follow.
Then come that many whole numbers, one on each line.
Exactly 0 is neither above nor below 0.
Round the average to 1 decimal place.

hint.think: Three answers need three variables, all set up before the loop and all updated inside it.
walk: Read one number on each turn of the loop.
Add it to the total of all of them, whatever it is.
Add it to the above-0 total only when it is above 0.
Add 1 to the count only when it is below 0.
Display the three answers after the loop.

questions.starter: # Three answers from one pass through the numbers

tests.why: The first line adds only the three numbers above 0, while the average uses all four.
Nothing is above 0, so the first line is 0, and that 0 still has to be displayed.
Exactly 0 counts as neither, so the first two lines stay at 0.
Three separate variables, so each answer is kept apart from the others.

questions.fb: One loop can keep as many running totals as you like, as long as each one has its own variable.
